passages.happening:
“Now the famine was still severe in the land” (verse 1). The grain from Egypt runs out, and Jacob tells his sons to go back and buy a little more (verse 2).

Judah reminds him of the Egyptian lord's warning: “You will not see my face again unless your brother is with you” (verse 3). Without Benjamin, they will not go (verses 4-5).

Jacob asks, “Why did you tell the man you had another brother?” (verse 6). They explain that the man asked them straight out (verse 7).

Then Judah speaks to his father. “Send the boy with me, and we will go at once, so that we may live and not die” (verse 8). “I will guarantee his safety. You may hold me personally responsible” (verse 9). If he does not bring Benjamin back, “then may I bear the guilt before you all my life” (verse 9).
passages.hearers:
Reuben tried in the last chapter, with a wild offer (42:37). Jacob said no. Now Judah steps forward, and his father listens.

Remember who Judah is. He was the brother who said, ‘What profit will we gain?’ and sold Joseph for silver (37:26-27). Then he left his family and wronged his daughter-in-law Tamar, until he admitted, ‘She is more righteous than I’ (38:26). Something has been changing in him.

Listen to his offer. He does not offer someone else's sons, as Reuben did. He offers himself. ‘I will guarantee his safety’ is a word from the world of debts. It means to stand surety: to promise to pay if the other person cannot. Judah makes himself answerable for Benjamin's life.

Why do they call Benjamin ‘the boy’? He was born before Joseph was sold, so he is a grown man by now. The Hebrew word for ‘boy’ covers a wide range, from a baby to a young man. Joseph was called that at seventeen (37:2). In Jacob's mouth it is also a father's word for his youngest, most protected son.

And Judah is blunt about the time: ‘If we had not delayed, we could have come and gone twice by now’ (verse 10). Hunger does not wait for an old man's fear.
passages.later: The New Testament uses this same idea of a guarantee for Jesus, who came from Judah's tribe: “our Lord descended from Judah” (Hebrews 7:14), and “Jesus has become the guarantee of a better covenant” (Hebrews 7:22). Genesis does not present Judah's pledge as a prophecy. But it shows the shape the gospel fills: one who binds himself to bear the cost so that another may come home.
passages.asks: Judah put himself on the line for his brother, the kind of brother he once sold. Ask whether there is someone you are willing to stand behind at a cost to yourself. Then ask whether your promises cost you anything.

passages.t: ‘If I am bereaved, I am bereaved’
passages.happening:
Jacob gives in. “If it must be so, then do this” (verse 11). They are to take a gift for the man: “a little balm and a little honey, spices and myrrh, pistachios and almonds” (verse 11).

They are to take double the silver, to return what they found in their sacks. “Perhaps it was a mistake” (verse 12). And they are to take Benjamin (verse 13).

Then Jacob prays. “May God Almighty grant you mercy before the man, that he may release your other brother along with Benjamin. As for me, if I am bereaved, I am bereaved” (verse 14).
passages.hearers:
The gift is made of the best things Canaan grew. Balm and myrrh are sweet-smelling tree resins. Pistachios and almonds are nuts. In a famine, these were small luxuries. A gift went ahead of a request to a powerful man. Jacob did the same when he sent flocks ahead of him to Esau (32:20).

The first hearers would notice the list. ‘Spices, balm, and myrrh’ were the very goods the traders carried when they took Joseph down to Egypt as a slave (37:25). Now the same kind of cargo goes down to Joseph again, as a gift.

Jacob prays to ‘God Almighty’, in Hebrew El Shaddai. It is the name God used when he promised Jacob a nation and the land (35:11). Jacob holds on to that old promise.

Then he lets go. ‘If I am bereaved, I am bereaved.’ To be bereaved is to lose someone you love to death. It is not quite faith, and not quite despair. It is an old man who can no longer protect his son, handing him over.
passages.later:
Queen Esther speaks in almost the same way when she goes to the king to plead for her people: “And if I perish, I perish!” (Esther 4:16).

Proverbs notes the old custom of gifts: “A man's gift opens doors for him, and brings him before great men” (Proverbs 18:16).
passages.asks: Jacob finally let go of the son he could not keep safe. Ask what you are holding on to so tightly that it is starving the people around you. Then ask whether you can pray Jacob's prayer, and put it in God's hands.

passages.happening:
The brothers go down with the gifts, the double silver and Benjamin, “and stood before Joseph” (verse 15).

When Joseph sees Benjamin, he tells his steward to take the men to his house and prepare a meal, “for they shall dine with me at noon” (verse 16).

The brothers are terrified. “They intend to overpower us and take us as slaves, along with our donkeys” (verse 18). At the door they tell the steward about the silver in their sacks. “We do not know who put our silver in our sacks” (verse 22).

“It is fine,” says the steward. “Do not be afraid. Your God, the God of your father, gave you the treasure that was in your sacks. I received your silver” (verse 23). Then he brings Simeon out to them. He gives them water to wash their feet and food for their donkeys (verse 24).
passages.hearers:
A steward was the man in charge of a great household: its guests, its money and its meals. Egyptian officials had them.

The brothers expect punishment at every turn. They are invited to dinner, and they think it is a trap. They rush to explain the silver before anyone has accused them. Guilty people often live like this, waiting for the blow.

Notice their fear: ‘take us as slaves’. That is what they did to Joseph. The thing they fear most is the thing they once did.

The steward's answer is full of meaning he does not know. ‘Your God, the God of your father, gave you the treasure.’ He is right. The silver was a gift, from Joseph and, behind Joseph, from God.

Water to wash the feet and food for the animals were signs of a proper welcome, as when Abraham welcomed his three visitors (18:4). The men who feared chains are treated as guests.
passages.later:
A psalm speaks of this kind of welcome: “You prepare a table before me in the presence of my enemies” (Psalm 23:5). Peter writes to anxious people, “Cast all your anxiety on Him, because He cares for you” (1 Peter 5:7).

Jesus noticed when a host gave no water for his feet (Luke 7:44). The welcome mattered.
passages.asks: The brothers expected punishment and were given a meal. Ask whether you expect God to deal with you as your guilt deserves. Then hear the steward's words again, ‘Do not be afraid’, and ask what it would mean to believe them.

passages.happening:
Joseph comes home. The brothers give him their gift and bow to the ground (verse 26). He asks about their father: “Is he still alive?” (verse 27). They bow again (verse 28).

Joseph sees Benjamin, “his own mother's son” (verse 29). “May God be gracious to you, my son,” he says (verse 29). Then he hurries out, “because he was moved to tears for his brother, and he went to a private room to weep” (verse 30). He washes his face, comes back and says, “Serve the meal” (verse 31).

Joseph, his brothers and the Egyptians eat at separate tables, “because the Egyptians would not eat with the Hebrews, since that was detestable to them” (verse 32).

The brothers are seated in order of age, “and the men looked at one another in astonishment” (verse 33). Benjamin's portion is five times larger than anyone else's. “So they feasted and drank freely with Joseph” (verse 34).
passages.hearers:
Eleven brothers now bow before Joseph. In his second dream eleven stars bowed down (37:9). It has happened.

Joseph's first question is about his father. And when he sees Benjamin, his only full brother, the son of his own mother Rachel, he cannot hold himself together. This is the second time he weeps in secret. He will weep again and again in these chapters.

Why separate tables? The narrator says Egyptians would not eat with Hebrews. Much later, in the 400s BC, the Greek writer Herodotus said something similar about Egyptians and Greeks. He wrote that Egyptians would not use a Greek's knife or cooking pot. That is a different people and a much later time, but it shows that such rules of eating apart were real. Joseph probably sits apart because of his rank as well.

Then the seating. Eleven brothers are placed in order of birth, oldest to youngest. How could an Egyptian know? The brothers stare at each other.

And Benjamin is given five times as much. Many readers think this is a quiet test. Years ago the brothers hated a favored son of Rachel. Will the old jealousy flare up again? This time the text records no anger at all. They eat and drink together.
passages.later:
Jesus taught about who sits where at a feast, and told his hearers to “invite the poor, the crippled, the lame, and the blind” (Luke 14:13).

Paul writes of a love that comes to people while they are still in the wrong: “While we were still sinners, Christ died for us” (Romans 5:8). The brothers eat at the table of the man they sold, and they do not yet know it.
passages.asks: Benjamin was given five times more, and this time his brothers did not resent it. Ask how you respond when someone else is favored. Then ask whether you can rejoice at another's gift without counting your own.
